questions.question: You need to deploy a stateless web application that automatically scales from zero to millions of requests with no infrastructure management. Which GCP compute service is the best fit?
options: App Engine Flexible with vCPU-based autoscaling
GKE Standard with cluster and pod autoscaling enabled
Compute Engine managed instance groups with autoscaler
Cloud Run with concurrency-based request scaling
questions.explanation: Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform that scales containers from zero to many based on incoming requests and concurrency, with no infrastructure to manage. App Engine Flexible runs on Compute Engine VMs and keeps at least one instance alive — it cannot scale to zero. GKE Standard requires you to size and operate the node pools. Compute Engine MIGs need autoscaler configuration plus base instances; scaling to zero is not the default and you still own the OS.

questions.question: A developer needs to grant a service account the minimum permissions to read objects from a specific Cloud Storage bucket. Which IAM role should be granted at the bucket level?
options: roles/storage.objectCreator
roles/storage.objectViewer
roles/storage.objectAdmin
roles/storage.legacyBucketReader
questions.explanation: roles/storage.objectViewer grants storage.objects.get and storage.objects.list on the bucket's objects, satisfying read-only least privilege. roles/storage.objectCreator allows uploads only and does not grant read. roles/storage.objectAdmin adds write and delete on objects, far more than needed. roles/storage.legacyBucketReader grants metadata read on the bucket itself but does not grant access to read the object data.

questions.question: You are creating a Compute Engine VM that must call BigQuery and Cloud Storage APIs without any credential file stored on disk. What is the recommended approach?
options: Copy a JSON service-account key onto the VM disk and load it from the application
Set the service-account credentials in startup-script environment variables
Attach a dedicated service account to the VM and grant it the required roles
Use the default Compute Engine service account with the project Editor role
questions.explanation: Attach a dedicated service account to the VM. Workloads on the VM authenticate to Google Cloud APIs by retrieving short-lived access tokens from the instance metadata server — no key file is required. Storing a JSON key on the disk creates a long-lived credential at risk of theft or accidental commit. Putting the key in startup-script env vars is equivalent to disk storage and is logged. The default compute service account with project Editor is over-privileged and violates least privilege.

questions.question: Which Cloud Storage class is the most cost-effective for data that is accessed roughly once a year while still offering 99.9% (multi-region 99.95%) typical availability?
options: Archive
Coldline
Standard
Nearline
questions.explanation: Coldline targets data accessed at most once every 90 days and has a 90-day minimum storage duration, making it the cheapest fit for once-a-year reads while still hitting the standard availability target. Archive is cheaper at rest but has a 365-day minimum storage duration and higher retrieval costs, so a single early read can cost more than Coldline. Nearline targets monthly access (30-day minimum). Standard targets frequent access and is the most expensive option at rest.

questions.question: You need to allow internet traffic on TCP port 443 to a fleet of VMs in your VPC. No firewall rule for port 443 exists yet. What must you do?
options: Establish a VPC peering link to route inbound 443 traffic from the public internet
Assign each VM an external IP address and enable IP forwarding on the instances
Create an ingress firewall rule allowing TCP:443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the target VMs
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway and use it as an inbound HTTPS reverse proxy
questions.explanation: GCP VPCs apply an implicit deny-all on ingress, so you must create an explicit ingress firewall rule allowing TCP:443 from source 0.0.0.0/0 (typically scoped to target tags or service accounts). Assigning external IPs only gives instances internet addressability — it does not open any port through the firewall. Cloud NAT only provides source-NAT for outbound flows; it does not accept unsolicited inbound traffic. VPC peering connects two private VPCs and cannot peer with the public internet.

questions.question: Your GKE cluster must run a log-collector pod on every node, including nodes added later by the autoscaler. Which Kubernetes workload type fits this requirement?
options: Deployment with the replica count pinned to the current node count
DaemonSet that schedules one pod on every matching node
StatefulSet with per-node anti-affinity rules and persistent volumes
CronJob that runs hourly with hostNetwork enabled on each cluster node
questions.explanation: A DaemonSet places exactly one pod on every node (or every node matching its selector) and automatically schedules a pod on newly added nodes. This is the standard pattern for log shippers, monitoring agents and CNI plugins. A Deployment with a fixed replica count drifts as the node count changes. StatefulSet anti-affinity can spread pods but is not guaranteed to track every node. CronJobs run on a schedule, not continuously on every node.

questions.question: A platform engineer needs to list every Compute Engine VM in project `prod-network` that lives in zone `us-central1-a` using a single gcloud command. Which command does this?
options: gcloud beta compute regions describe us-central1 --project=prod-network
gcloud compute vms list prod-network us-central1-a
gcloud projects describe prod-network --include-instances
gcloud compute instances list --project=prod-network --filter="zone:us-central1-a"
questions.explanation: `gcloud compute instances list` enumerates VM instances and accepts `--project` plus a `--filter` (or `--zones=`) to scope the results to a single zone. The subgroup is `instances`, not `vms` — `gcloud compute vms` is not a real command. `gcloud compute regions describe` returns metadata about a region object, not a list of VMs. `gcloud projects describe` returns project metadata only and has no `--include-instances` flag.

questions.question: You need a fully managed relational database service on GCP that is wire-compatible with MySQL 8.0. Which product should you choose?
options: Firestore in Native mode
Cloud SQL for MySQL
Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL is Google's fully managed relational database service and offers MySQL (5.6/5.7/8.0), PostgreSQL and SQL Server engines — applications can connect with standard MySQL drivers. Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database but uses its own SQL dialect and is not wire-compatible with MySQL. Cloud Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store. Firestore is a document-oriented NoSQL database with no relational schema.

questions.question: A team wants to be alerted whenever the CPU utilization of their Compute Engine VMs exceeds 80% for more than 5 minutes. Which GCP feature provides this?
options: Cloud Audit Logs with notification channels attached to log entries
Error Reporting with email subscriptions for high-severity issues
Cloud Trace alerting on latency spans for long-running requests
Cloud Monitoring with an alerting policy on the CPU utilization metric
questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring (formerly Stackdriver) collects metrics from GCP resources and lets you define alerting policies with metric conditions, duration thresholds and notification channels — exactly the requirement here. Cloud Audit Logs record API activity, not utilization metrics; alerts on them would not fire on CPU usage. Cloud Trace analyses request latency spans. Error Reporting aggregates application exceptions, not host metrics.

questions.question: A subnet hosts VMs with no public IPs that must reach the public internet for OS updates and SaaS APIs while remaining unreachable from inbound flows. You want a managed regional resource that source-NATs the outbound flows behind shared addresses. Which GCP resource fits?
options: Cloud Armor
An external HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front of the subnet
Cloud Router with custom advertised routes
Cloud NAT attached to the VPC and region
questions.explanation: Cloud NAT performs source NAT for instances without external IP addresses, allowing outbound connections while accepting no unsolicited inbound traffic. Cloud Armor is an L7 WAF in front of HTTP(S) load balancers and does not provide outbound NAT. An external load balancer handles inbound traffic. Cloud Router exchanges BGP routes between a VPC and on-premises networks; it is required as the control plane for Cloud NAT but is not itself the NAT data plane.

questions.question: You need to deploy a containerized application that requires persistent disk storage per replica and must maintain a stable network identity. Which Kubernetes workload type is most appropriate?
options: Deployment with a single PersistentVolumeClaim shared by all replicas
StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates and a headless Service
DaemonSet with a hostPath volume mount on each node
ReplicaSet placed behind an external LoadBalancer Service
questions.explanation: StatefulSets provide stable, predictable pod names (myapp-0, myapp-1), ordered rollout and scale-down, and a per-pod PVC via volumeClaimTemplates. Combined with a headless Service, each pod gets a stable DNS name — the canonical pattern for stateful workloads like databases. Deployments give pods random hashes and share or recycle a single PVC. DaemonSets are for per-node agents, not application replicas with stable identity. A bare ReplicaSet has no identity or storage guarantees beyond what its pod template provides.

questions.question: Which load balancer should you choose to route HTTP/HTTPS traffic globally to backends in multiple regions with built-in DDoS protection?
options: Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer (regional, L4)
Regional External TCP/UDP Load Balancer (L4)
Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer (L7)
Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancer (regional, L7)
questions.explanation: The Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer is a Layer 7 proxy on Google's global front-end that steers each request to the closest healthy backend across regions and integrates with Cloud Armor for WAF and DDoS protection. Internal load balancers only serve clients inside the VPC. Regional external balancers terminate in a single region and cannot route across regions natively.

questions.question: A team operates multiple environments (dev, staging, prod) for the same application. What is the recommended GCP resource-hierarchy approach to isolate billing, quotas and access control per environment?
options: Place each environment in its own VPC inside a single shared project
Use a separate GCP project per environment under a common folder
Use a separate service account per environment in one shared project
Apply labels and folders to tag resources with their environment
questions.explanation: Projects are GCP's primary isolation boundary: each project has its own IAM policy, billing account assignment, quotas and audit trail. A separate project per environment is the recommended pattern, often grouped under an `environments/` folder for shared IAM and Org Policy. VPC separation does not isolate IAM or billing. Distinct service accounts in one project still inherit that project's IAM bindings. Labels are metadata used for filtering and billing breakdowns, not an isolation boundary.

questions.question: You need to store structured, schemaless JSON documents with real-time sync for a mobile application. Which GCP database is the best fit?
options: Cloud Spanner
Firestore in Native mode
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
Cloud Bigtable
questions.explanation: Firestore in Native mode is Google's serverless document database with native real-time listeners, offline persistence on mobile/web SDKs and automatic horizontal scaling — purpose-built for mobile and web apps. Cloud Bigtable is a wide-column store for analytics and high-throughput time-series workloads, with no document model or real-time listeners. Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner are relational databases requiring a fixed schema and do not provide live mobile sync.

questions.question: A team enables Object Versioning on a Cloud Storage bucket. A user then overwrites `report.pdf` with an empty file and afterwards deletes the live object. What happens to the older states of `report.pdf`?
options: Each prior version is encrypted with a unique customer-managed key but the bytes are not retained for retrieval
Every prior state is purged on overwrite; only the latest live object is kept, just like a versionless bucket
Only deletions are retained as noncurrent versions; overwrites are not preserved if the writer has object permissions
Both the overwritten and the deleted prior states are kept as noncurrent versions, retrievable until a lifecycle rule deletes them
questions.explanation: Object Versioning keeps the previous state of an object as a noncurrent version on both overwrite and delete. Each noncurrent version carries its original generation number and can be listed, restored or permanently deleted, typically aged out by an Object Lifecycle Management rule. Versioning does not change encryption, replication or mutability — making objects immutable requires a retention policy or object hold, not versioning.

questions.question: You need to run a Bash script every day at 02:00 UTC on GCP with no persistent VM. Which is the most cost-effective approach?
options: Keep a Compute Engine VM running 24/7 with a crontab entry for the job
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function or Cloud Run job at 02:00
Run a GKE CronJob on a small dedicated node pool just for the schedule
Deploy an App Engine Standard service with a `cron.yaml` schedule
questions.explanation: Cloud Scheduler firing a Cloud Function or Cloud Run job is the serverless, pay-per-execution pattern for scheduled work — you pay only for execution time, not idle hours. A 24/7 Compute Engine VM is wasteful for a once-daily job. A dedicated GKE node pool carries minimum control-plane and node costs even when idle. App Engine `cron.yaml` works but locks you into App Engine Standard runtimes and instance keep-alive billing.

questions.question: A GKE cluster has pods stuck in `Pending` because no existing node has enough memory to schedule them. You want the cluster to automatically add nodes to existing node pools when this happens. Which feature should you enable?
options: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
Node Auto-Provisioning
Vertical Pod Autoscaler
Cluster Autoscaler
questions.explanation: Cluster Autoscaler watches for unschedulable pods and adds nodes to existing node pools to fit them (and removes underused nodes). HPA changes pod replica counts, not the node count. VPA adjusts CPU/memory requests on individual pods but cannot add capacity. Node Auto-Provisioning creates entirely new node pools when no existing pool's shape fits — useful, but the question asks specifically about adding nodes to existing pools, which is Cluster Autoscaler's job.

questions.question: A GKE operator needs to create a new Kubernetes namespace called `production` in the cluster that their `kubectl` context currently points to. Which single command does this?
options: gcloud container clusters create production
kubectl create namespace production
kubectl apply --namespace=production
kubectl get namespaces production
questions.explanation: `kubectl create namespace production` (short form `kubectl create ns production`) creates a new Namespace object in the active cluster. `gcloud container clusters create` creates a new GKE cluster, not a Namespace inside an existing cluster. `kubectl apply --namespace=production` requires a manifest input and only sets the namespace flag on the apply — it does not create the namespace if it does not already exist. `kubectl get` is read-only and lists or shows resources, never creates them.

questions.question: You need to connect your on-premises network to a GCP VPC with dedicated 10 Gbps bandwidth, low latency and a service-level agreement. Which connectivity option fits?
options: Cloud VPN over the public internet using IPsec tunnels
Cloud NAT with a private routing table to on-premises
Partner Interconnect through a supported service provider
Dedicated Interconnect via cross-connect in a Google colocation facility
questions.explanation: Dedicated Interconnect provides a direct physical fibre cross-connect between your on-premises router (in a Google colocation facility) and Google's edge network. It supports 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps circuits with a 99.9% SLA (99.99% with the recommended redundant topology). Cloud VPN traverses the public internet and offers no bandwidth SLA. Partner Interconnect uses a service-provider link with bandwidth options below or above 10 Gbps but is a managed-partner topology, not a direct cross-connect. Cloud NAT is an outbound-only service.

questions.question: An admin wants to grant an IAM role to every member of their Google Workspace organisation in a single binding — employees, contractors and future hires alike — without having to maintain a group. Which principal identifier should they reference on the binding?
options: allUsers
allAuthenticatedUsers
domain:example.com
group:everyone@example.com
questions.explanation: The `domain:DOMAIN_NAME` principal grants the role to every Google account in the named Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain, with no group to manage. `allUsers` grants access to anyone on the internet including unauthenticated callers — far too broad. `allAuthenticatedUsers` covers any Google-authenticated user globally, not just your company. `group:` requires that an actual Google Group exist and be populated with the right members; it is not the domain-wide identifier.

questions.question: You deployed a Cloud Run service and need to split traffic so that 90% goes to revision v2 and 10% goes to revision v1 for canary testing. How do you configure this?
options: Configure Cloud CDN to send a percentage of traffic to each Cloud Run revision
Place a global HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front and assign weighted backends per revision
Deploy v1 and v2 as two separate Cloud Run services behind a load balancer
Use built-in traffic splitting on the Cloud Run service with weights per revision
questions.explanation: Cloud Run has native, per-service traffic splitting between revisions. Set weights with `gcloud run services update-traffic --to-revisions=v2=90,v1=10` (or use the Console). This is the canonical canary mechanism and requires no external load balancer or CDN. Cloud CDN caches HTTP responses and does not weight traffic. Splitting via a load balancer or two separate services is more complex and unnecessary when revisions of the same service already support weighting.

questions.question: Your application runs on a Compute Engine VM and writes its logs to local files under /var/log/myapp. You want those entries to flow into Cloud Logging. What is the recommended approach?
options: Write logs to /var/log/syslog so Compute Engine ingests them automatically
Install and configure the Cloud Ops Agent on the VM and point it at the log files
Rely on Compute Engine to stream system and application logs without any agent
Write logs to a Cloud Storage bucket and import them into Cloud Logging on a schedule
questions.explanation: Compute Engine VMs do not forward application or system logs to Cloud Logging by default. You install the Cloud Ops Agent (which supersedes the legacy Logging and Monitoring agents), configure receivers that tail the relevant log files, and the agent streams entries into Cloud Logging and metrics into Cloud Monitoring. GCP-managed runtimes such as GKE, Cloud Run and App Engine emit logs without an agent; raw Compute Engine does not.

questions.question: A Cloud SQL primary is hot on read traffic. You want to offload read-only queries without rewriting the application's data layer. What should you add?
options: Upgrade the primary instance to a larger machine type
Migrate the workload to Cloud Spanner for horizontal read scale-out
Add Memorystore for Redis in front as a read-through cache
Add a Cloud SQL read replica and point read traffic at its connection string
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL read replicas are asynchronously replicated copies of the primary that serve read-only queries. The application just connects to the replica's connection string for reads — no schema or SQL-dialect changes. Upgrading the primary helps but still uses a single instance and is more expensive. Memorystore requires application-level cache code and cache-invalidation handling. Migrating to Spanner is a major schema and SQL-dialect change, not a quick offload.

questions.question: Your GKE workload needs to authenticate to a Cloud SQL database. What is the recommended, secure way to provide that authentication?
options: Hard-code the database password in the Deployment YAML manifest
Store the database password in a Kubernetes Secret mounted as an environment variable
Use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar with Workload Identity bound to a GCP service account
Grant the cluster's default node service account the project-wide Editor role
questions.explanation: The recommended pattern is the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy (deployed as a sidecar) combined with Workload Identity, which maps a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a GCP service account that holds `roles/cloudsql.client`. The proxy provides an encrypted IAM-authenticated channel — no static database password is stored in the cluster. Plain Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded and visible to anyone with `get` on Secrets in that namespace. Granting Editor at the node pool level is dramatically over-privileged.

questions.question: Which Compute Engine pricing model automatically reduces the cost of standard VMs that run for a significant portion of the billing month, requires no upfront commitment and never reclaims the instance?
options: Committed Use Discounts (1- or 3-year commitment)
Preemptible VMs (legacy interruptible instances)
Sustained Use Discounts (automatic monthly)
Spot VMs (current interruptible instances)
questions.explanation: Sustained Use Discounts apply automatically to standard Compute Engine instances that run for more than 25% of a billing month, growing as usage increases. There is no commitment to make and no risk of preemption. CUDs require a 1- or 3-year commitment in exchange for a deeper discount. Preemptible and Spot VMs are deeply discounted but Google can reclaim them at any time, so they fail the 'never reclaimed' part of the question.

questions.question: You need to deploy an application on App Engine that receives bursty traffic and must scale to zero instances when idle to minimize cost. Which App Engine configuration meets this?
options: App Engine Flexible with manual scaling
App Engine Standard with automatic scaling
App Engine Flexible with automatic scaling
App Engine Standard with manual scaling
questions.explanation: App Engine Standard with automatic scaling can scale to zero instances when there is no traffic, so you pay nothing during idle periods. App Engine Flexible runs on Compute Engine VMs and keeps at least one instance alive at all times — it cannot scale to zero. Manual scaling pins a fixed number of instances regardless of load, defeating the cost goal.

questions.question: A central platform team wants to enforce constraints on which APIs, regions and service-account behaviours can be used by every project under an Organisation — for example denying `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` org-wide — and have those constraints inherit from the Org or a Folder down to each Project. Which service is this?
options: Organization Policy Service
Cloud Asset Inventory
Security Command Center
Cloud Audit Logs
questions.explanation: Organization Policy Service lets you define and enforce constraints on how GCP resources can be configured — for example forbidding external IPs on VMs, restricting allowed locations, or disabling service-account key creation. Policies attach at the organization, folder or project node and inherit downward; they sit on top of IAM rather than replacing it. Cloud Asset Inventory is a read-only inventory and change history; it can find violations but cannot prevent them. Security Command Center is a posture dashboard that consumes findings, not a policy enforcer. Cloud Audit Logs record actions after the fact and are not preventive.

questions.question: A Compute Engine VM has been accidentally deleted. You took a snapshot of its boot disk two hours before the deletion. What is the correct way to bring back a running VM from that snapshot?
options: Restore directly from the snapshot — it re-creates the original VM and all its metadata
Use Cloud Backup and DR to restore the original VM from the snapshot in place
Create a new persistent disk from the snapshot, then create a new VM using that disk as its boot disk
Treat the snapshot as a diagnostic artifact only — it cannot be booted into a VM
questions.explanation: A Compute Engine snapshot is a disk image, not a VM image. To recover, you create a new persistent disk from the snapshot (`gcloud compute disks create … --source-snapshot=…`) and then create a new VM that uses it as the boot disk (or use `gcloud compute instances create … --source-snapshot=…`). Snapshots do not preserve VM-level metadata like network tags, labels or attached service accounts — those must be reapplied. Cloud Backup and DR is a separate product for VM-level backup and is not how raw snapshots are consumed.

questions.question: You want to run complex SQL queries with joins and aggregations against structured log data currently in Cloud Logging. What is the standard pattern?
options: Export logs to BigQuery via a log sink and query them there with standard SQL
Use Cloud Monitoring's Metrics Explorer to write SQL over log entries
Use Cloud Trace to query structured log payloads with a SQL dialect
Query the logs directly in Cloud Logging using BigQuery SQL syntax in the UI
questions.explanation: Log sinks route Cloud Logging entries to destinations such as BigQuery, Cloud Storage and Pub/Sub. Routing to BigQuery lets you run full standard SQL — joins, window functions and aggregations — across log data at scale. Cloud Logging's Log Analytics offers SQL-style queries for ad-hoc inspection on log buckets, but BigQuery remains the destination for heavy analytics joining logs against other tables. Cloud Monitoring's Metrics Explorer queries time-series metrics with MQL/PromQL, not SQL. Cloud Trace analyses request spans, not logs.

questions.question: You need to give an external auditor read-only access to every Cloud Logging entry in a project, including Data Access audit logs. What is the minimum predefined IAM role that satisfies this?
options: roles/logging.privateLogViewer
roles/logging.admin
roles/logging.viewer
roles/viewer
questions.explanation: roles/logging.privateLogViewer grants read access to all log entries including Data Access audit logs, which are treated as private. roles/logging.viewer only exposes Admin Activity and System Event audit logs and would hide Data Access entries. roles/viewer is a broad project-level read role that exceeds least privilege. roles/logging.admin grants full control over Cloud Logging — sinks, configuration and deletion — which is far more than read-only.

questions.question: A Cloud Storage bucket should automatically delete every object older than 30 days. What is the simplest, native way to enforce that?
options: Run a Cloud Scheduler job that calls the Storage API daily to find and delete old objects
Configure a bucket retention policy plus an object hold to enforce the maximum age
Wire a Cloud Function on object creation that deletes the object after 30 days
Add an Object Lifecycle Management rule with `age=30 days` and the Delete action
questions.explanation: Object Lifecycle Management evaluates rules against each object daily and performs the configured action — here a `Delete` action with an `age` condition of 30 days. It is built-in, requires no code and incurs no extra compute. Bucket retention policies do the opposite: they prevent deletion before the retention period elapses. A Scheduler-plus-Function pipeline reimplements functionality the platform already provides, adding cost and operational risk.

questions.question: A team enables Uniform bucket-level access on a Cloud Storage bucket. Afterwards, attempts to set per-object ACLs are rejected. What does enabling this setting actually do?
options: Disables legacy per-object ACLs on the bucket and enforces that access is governed only by IAM at the bucket level
Encrypts every object with a customer-managed key and rejects reads from outside the customer's VPC Service Controls perimeter
Replicates the bucket across regions transparently with bucket-level consistency rather than per-object consistency
Converts the bucket to the Nearline storage class so that reads are billed per access while writes remain free for 30 days
questions.explanation: Uniform bucket-level access (UBA) turns off legacy per-object ACLs and enforces that access decisions are made solely by Cloud IAM policy at the bucket level. This collapses two permission systems into one and is required by several compliance frameworks. UBA does not change the bucket's location, replication, storage class or default encryption — those are independent settings.

questions.question: You need to alert the billing admin when project spending reaches 80% of the monthly budget. Which GCP feature handles this?
options: Cloud Monitoring with a custom alert on a billing metric
A Pub/Sub subscription on a built-in billing-events topic
Cloud Billing budgets with threshold-based notification rules
A Looker Studio billing dashboard with email alerts
questions.explanation: Cloud Billing budgets let you define a spending threshold against a billing account, project or set of services and configure email plus Pub/Sub notifications at custom percentages (for example 50%, 80%, 100%). Cloud Monitoring is for resource performance metrics, not billing thresholds. Pub/Sub is a delivery channel a budget alert can publish to but is not itself the threshold engine. Looker Studio renders dashboards and lacks built-in alerting on budget thresholds.

questions.question: A microservices application on GKE needs service-to-service mTLS encryption and traffic policies — canary, retries, circuit breaking — applied transparently without modifying application code. What should you deploy?
options: Anthos Service Mesh (managed Istio) with sidecar injection
Cloud Endpoints as an API gateway in front of each service
Cloud Armor security policies attached to each Pod
Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the GKE workloads
questions.explanation: Anthos Service Mesh (managed Istio) injects an Envoy sidecar into each pod and transparently adds mTLS, traffic management (weighted routing, retries, circuit breakers) and rich observability to east-west service-to-service traffic — with no application code changes. Cloud Endpoints manages north-south API contracts at the edge. IAP authenticates end users to apps, it does not manage pod-to-pod policy. Cloud Armor protects external HTTP load balancers from web attacks; it does not sit between pods.

questions.question: You need to give a VM in Project A access to a Cloud Storage bucket in Project B. What is the correct, least-privileged approach?
options: Cross-project access is blocked by default; open a quota or support ticket to permit it
Share Project A owner credentials with a service account in Project B
Grant the VM's service account the required role on the bucket in Project B
Establish VPC Network Peering between Project A and Project B networks
questions.explanation: IAM bindings can name any principal — including a service account from another project — on any resource. Grant the VM's service account the role it needs (for example `roles/storage.objectViewer`) on the specific bucket in Project B. Cross-project IAM is the standard, supported pattern; no quota change or peering is required. Sharing owner credentials is a serious anti-pattern that violates account ownership. VPC peering connects networks but does not authorise IAM access to a bucket.

questions.question: A brand-new GCP project needs to use the Pub/Sub API. What must you do before any API call will succeed?
options: Enable the Pub/Sub API in the project via Cloud Console or `gcloud services enable pubsub.googleapis.com`
Open a support ticket to ask Google to enable the Pub/Sub API for the project
Wait for Pub/Sub to become available automatically once the project's billing account is linked
Create a Pub/Sub-specific service account first; that automatically activates the API
questions.explanation: Most GCP APIs are disabled by default in a new project. You must explicitly enable each one — Console > APIs & Services > Enable APIs, or `gcloud services enable pubsub.googleapis.com` — before any caller, including service accounts, can use it. Creating a service account does not auto-enable APIs, billing alone does not activate them, and no support ticket is required: enablement is self-service.

questions.question: You need to deploy infrastructure across multiple GCP projects using a repeatable, version-controlled, declarative configuration that also works across other clouds. Which tool is most appropriate?
options: Cloud Deployment Manager YAML templates
gcloud Bash scripts stored in Cloud Source Repositories
Cloud Build pipelines with Bash `gcloud` deploy steps
Terraform with the official Google Cloud provider
questions.explanation: Terraform is the industry-standard declarative IaC tool with first-class GCP and multi-cloud providers, state management, plan/apply workflows and a rich module ecosystem. Cloud Deployment Manager is GCP-only and Google has marked it for end of support. gcloud shell scripts are imperative, not declarative, and do not track state. Cloud Build is a CI/CD runner that can execute Terraform but is not itself an IaC tool.

questions.question: Which GCP service is the fully managed, globally scalable publish-subscribe messaging system used as the default for asynchronous event ingestion and streaming pipelines?
options: Cloud Pub/Sub
Cloud Tasks
Datastream
Pub/Sub Lite
questions.explanation: Cloud Pub/Sub is Google's fully managed global pub/sub system for event ingestion and streaming pipelines, with at-least-once delivery and no capacity provisioning. Pub/Sub Lite is a lower-cost zonal product where you provision throughput capacity yourself; it shares some semantics but is not the global default. Cloud Tasks is for HTTP task execution with explicit per-task control and scheduling, not topic-based pub/sub. Datastream is a managed change-data-capture service that streams database changes — not general-purpose messaging.

questions.question: A GCP customer with many projects across departments wants an intermediate node above Projects where IAM and Organization Policy can be applied to a group of projects collectively (e.g. 'Engineering'), with sub-nodes mirroring sub-departments. Which feature provides this?
options: Label
VPC Service Controls perimeter
Budget
Folder
questions.explanation: Folders sit between the Organization and Project nodes in the hierarchy (Organization > Folders > Projects > Resources). IAM bindings and Organization Policies attached at a folder inherit to every child project, simplifying governance for large estates, and folders can nest to mirror sub-departments. Labels are free-form key/value tags on resources for filtering and billing breakdowns — they do not create a hierarchy or scope IAM. A VPC Service Controls perimeter is a data-exfiltration boundary around APIs, not a hierarchy node. A Budget is a billing alert primitive.

questions.question: You must encrypt a Cloud SQL database with an encryption key that your team creates, controls and can rotate. Which encryption option fits?
options: Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) backed by Cloud KMS
Google-managed encryption keys (default at-rest encryption)
Customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK) provided per request
Transparent Data Encryption configured inside the database engine
questions.explanation: Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS let you create, rotate, disable and audit the key that protects the Cloud SQL instance while Google still manages the underlying encryption operations. Google-managed encryption is the default but gives you no control over the key material. CSEK applies only to Compute Engine persistent disks and Cloud Storage, not Cloud SQL. Cloud SQL does not expose engine-level TDE configuration to customers — the platform handles encryption-at-rest below the engine layer.

questions.question: You want to containerize a Node.js application and deploy it to Cloud Run from an automated CI/CD pipeline. Which combination of GCP services is the standard pattern?
options: Compute Engine with Docker and Cloud Scheduler triggering rolling updates
App Engine Standard with Cloud Source Repositories triggering auto-deploy on push
Cloud Build builds the image, pushes to Artifact Registry, then deploys to Cloud Run
GKE Autopilot with a GitOps controller pulling images from Artifact Registry
questions.explanation: The standard CI/CD pattern for Cloud Run is Cloud Build (build the container image, run tests) → Artifact Registry (store the image with vulnerability scanning) → Cloud Run (`gcloud run deploy`). Cloud Build triggers connect to GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab or Cloud Source Repositories so commits drive builds automatically. The other options describe pipelines for Compute Engine, App Engine or GKE — they don't target Cloud Run.

questions.question: A Kubernetes Deployment has 3 replicas. You apply a new container image. By default, how does Kubernetes perform the rollout?
options: Terminates all three old pods first, then creates three new pods together
Creates all three new pods first, then terminates the three old pods together
Replaces pods incrementally — new pods come up as old pods terminate (RollingUpdate)
Requires a manual approval step before each individual pod replacement during rollout
questions.explanation: Deployments default to the RollingUpdate strategy with `maxUnavailable=25%` and `maxSurge=25%`. New pods come up while old pods are torn down so service capacity is preserved throughout the rollout. Terminating every old pod before creating new ones is the `Recreate` strategy (which causes downtime) and is not the default. There is no built-in manual approval gate in the RollingUpdate strategy itself.

questions.question: You need to migrate a 5 TB PostgreSQL database from on-premises to Cloud SQL with continuous replication and minimal cutover downtime. Which GCP service is purpose-built for this?
options: Cloud Dataflow
Database Migration Service (DMS)
Cloud Data Fusion
Transfer Appliance
questions.explanation: Database Migration Service (DMS) provides managed, low-downtime migrations from MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle to Cloud SQL and AlloyDB. It performs an initial dump and then continuous logical replication, so cutover takes minutes. Cloud Dataflow runs general-purpose Apache Beam pipelines and is not a managed DB-to-DB replicator. Cloud Data Fusion is visual ETL/ELT for analytics, not OLTP migration. Transfer Appliance is for offline bulk file transfer, not live database replication.

questions.question: A platform team wants a fully managed in-memory cache for application session data and frequent lookups. They want a choice between a Redis-compatible engine and a Memcached-compatible engine without operating any nodes. Which GCP product provides this?
options: Cloud Memorystore
Cloud SQL
Cloud Spanner
Cloud Bigtable
questions.explanation: Cloud Memorystore is Google's fully managed in-memory data store, offering Redis and Memcached engines for application caching, session storage and low-latency leaderboards — patching, failover and provisioning are handled by GCP. Cloud SQL is a managed relational database, not an in-memory cache. Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database with strong consistency. Cloud Bigtable is a persistent wide-column NoSQL store for analytics and time-series workloads.

questions.question: After deploying a new version of your App Engine service, you want to verify it before routing any production traffic to it. Which App Engine feature supports this?
options: Deploy the new build to a separate App Engine app inside a sibling test project
Deploy the new version with `--no-promote` so it gets 0% traffic, test it via its version URL, then migrate traffic
Run the new build as a staging service in the same App Engine app fronted by a custom load-balancer rule
Use Cloud Armor rules to selectively block production traffic from reaching the new version until you sign off
questions.explanation: App Engine runs multiple versions of a service side by side. Deploying with `--no-promote` keeps the new version at 0% traffic; you reach it through its version-specific URL (e.g. `VERSION-dot-SERVICE-dot-PROJECT.appspot.com`) to verify, then gradually migrate or split traffic. This is the canonical App Engine canary / blue-green workflow built into the platform. The other approaches reimplement the same outcome with more moving parts.

questions.question: A pipeline publishes events to Cloud Pub/Sub. Engineers need the upper bound on the size of a single message they can publish without splitting it. What is that limit?
options: 10 MB per message
256 KB per message
1 MB per message
No fixed limit; the broker accepts any payload within the project's bandwidth quota
questions.explanation: Cloud Pub/Sub accepts messages up to 10 MB. For larger payloads the recommended pattern is to upload the data to Cloud Storage and publish only a reference (e.g. a GCS object URI) in the Pub/Sub message — keeping broker traffic small and subscribers cheap. The 256 KB and 1 MB figures are limits for other messaging systems (e.g. SNS and many Kafka deployments), not Pub/Sub. There is always a per-message limit; the broker is not unbounded.

questions.question: You need to prevent any VM in your organisation from being created with an external IP address. What is the most efficient, preventive approach?
options: Write a Cloud Function that strips external IPs in response to instance-create audit events
Apply a VPC firewall rule that blocks all egress at the organization level
Apply an Organization Policy with the `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess` constraint set to Deny All
Configure a Shared VPC with subnets that do not permit external IP assignment
questions.explanation: The `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess` list constraint, set to Deny All at the organization node, blocks VM creation with any external IP and inherits to every folder and project. This is preventive and requires no code. A Cloud Function reacting to audit events is reactive and leaves a window in which the VM exists with an external IP. Firewall rules govern traffic flow once an interface exists; they do not stop interface assignment. There is no built-in 'subnet flag that forbids external IP'.

questions.question: Which gcloud command connects you to a Compute Engine VM and handles SSH key management automatically, including via OS Login when it is enabled?
options: gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE_NAME
gcloud compute rdp INSTANCE_NAME --port=22
ssh -i ~/.ssh/google_compute_engine INSTANCE_NAME
gcloud compute connect INSTANCE_NAME --ssh
questions.explanation: `gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE_NAME` manages keys for you: with OS Login enabled it provisions your POSIX account and uploads your public key via OS Login, otherwise it pushes a short-lived key into instance metadata. It can also tunnel through Identity-Aware Proxy with `--tunnel-through-iap`. `gcloud compute rdp` is the Windows RDP variant. A raw `ssh -i …` works but you must distribute keys yourself. `gcloud compute connect` is not a real subcommand.

questions.question: A production GKE cluster must remain available if any single GCP zone fails. Which cluster configuration achieves this with the least operational complexity?
options: A single-zone cluster with high-memory nodes and PodDisruptionBudgets
A regional cluster with node pools spread across multiple zones in the region
A single-zone cluster with PodDisruptionBudgets enforced on every workload
Three separate single-zone clusters (one per zone) connected by Multi-Cluster Ingress
questions.explanation: A Regional GKE cluster runs replicated control-plane components across three zones in a region and lets you spread node pools across those zones. If one zone fails, the cluster keeps serving from the surviving zones with no manual intervention. Single-zone clusters have the zone as a single point of failure regardless of PDBs. A multi-cluster setup also survives zone failure but is significantly more complex and is not what the question asks for.

questions.question: A GKE team runs several HTTP backends and wants a single L7 entry point that routes by host and path to the right Service, with native TLS termination integrated with Google Cloud Load Balancing. Which Kubernetes object provides this on GKE?
options: Ingress
A Service of type ClusterIP
A Service of type LoadBalancer
NetworkPolicy
questions.explanation: An Ingress resource defines HTTP/HTTPS routing rules — host-based and path-based — and exposes multiple backend Services through a single external endpoint. On GKE an Ingress is realised by a Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer with native TLS termination. A ClusterIP Service is reachable only inside the cluster. A LoadBalancer Service provisions an L4 cloud load balancer per Service and cannot route by host or path. NetworkPolicy is for east-west pod-to-pod policy and has nothing to do with L7 ingress routing.

questions.question: Your team uses Terraform to manage GCP resources. Where should you store the Terraform state to enable team collaboration and prevent concurrent modification?
options: On each developer's local machine in the working directory
In a Git repository checked in alongside the Terraform code
In a Cloud Storage bucket with versioning and a Spanner-based external lock store
In a Cloud Storage bucket configured as the GCS remote backend
questions.explanation: The GCS remote backend stores Terraform state in a Cloud Storage bucket and provides automatic state locking using Cloud Storage's atomic object operations — no separate lock store is required. Local state cannot be shared between teammates. Committing state to Git is unsafe because state files routinely contain secrets and Git has no concurrency control. The 'Spanner-based external lock' option describes a legacy DynamoDB-style pattern from AWS and is not how the GCS backend works.

questions.question: Which GCP service caches HTTP(S) content at Google's global edge locations for backends behind the external HTTP(S) Load Balancer?
options: Cloud Armor
Cloud Endpoints
Cloud CDN
Traffic Director
questions.explanation: Cloud CDN integrates with the Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer to cache content at Google's edge points of presence, reducing latency for end users and origin load. Cloud Armor protects the same load balancer with WAF and DDoS controls but does not cache. Cloud Endpoints manages API contracts and gateway behaviour, not edge caching. Traffic Director is a managed service-mesh control plane for east-west service traffic.

questions.question: A Cloud Function is returning 'permission denied' when writing to Cloud Firestore. What is the first thing you should check?
options: Whether the Cloud Functions API is enabled in the project at all
The memory and CPU allocation configured on the Cloud Function
Whether the Firestore region matches the Cloud Function region
The IAM roles granted to the Cloud Function's runtime service account
questions.explanation: Cloud Functions run under a service account identity. By default that is the App Engine default service account (which has Editor) but best practice is a dedicated runtime SA with least privilege. A 'permission denied' on Firestore writes points to the runtime SA missing `roles/datastore.user` (or another role that grants the write). Whether the API is enabled would cause a different error (`SERVICE_DISABLED`), region mismatch causes latency but not permission errors, and memory/CPU caps do not produce IAM errors.

questions.question: An engineer is comparing Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy. Which statement correctly captures the difference between them?
options: Cloud Armor is a perimeter L7 WAF and DDoS protection layer for HTTP(S) load balancers; IAP enforces user-identity, group and device-context-based access to apps and VMs.
Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy are the same product marketed under different names for billing reasons in different regions.
Cloud Armor is for internal east-west micro-segmentation between workloads; IAP is the perimeter WAF protecting load balancers from web exploits.
Cloud Armor enforces user identity per request; IAP filters purely on IP allow-lists with no user awareness or device context.
questions.explanation: Cloud Armor is a perimeter WAF and DDoS-protection service for HTTP(S) and TCP/SSL load balancers, with WAF rules (OWASP Top-10), IP allow/deny lists and geo controls. Identity-Aware Proxy gates access based on user identity, group membership and device posture, replacing the need for a VPN for many internal apps. They are complementary, not alternatives, and often attach in front of the same external load balancer.

questions.question: You are creating a custom VPC network for a new project and choose 'Custom' subnet mode. What does this setting mean?
options: GCP automatically creates one /20 subnet in each region inside the VPC
No subnets are created automatically; you define each subnet's region and CIDR range manually
The VPC enables IPv6 addressing by default on every subnet you create in it
Custom mode allows overlapping IP ranges with other VPCs in the same project
questions.explanation: In Custom subnet mode the VPC ships with no subnets; you define each subnet's region and CIDR range manually, giving full control over IP planning. In Auto mode GCP creates one /20 subnet per region with predefined ranges. Custom is recommended for production to avoid IP overlaps that would block future VPC peering or hybrid connectivity. Subnet mode does not toggle IPv6 and does not change how IP overlap is detected with other VPCs.

questions.question: Which command correctly sets the default project and the default Compute Engine region for all subsequent gcloud commands in the active configuration?
options: gcloud set project=PROJECT_ID --compute-region=REGION --persist-config
gcloud init --project=PROJECT_ID --compute-region=REGION --skip-prompts
gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID; gcloud config set compute/region REGION
gcloud configure --default-project=PROJECT_ID --default-region=REGION --persist
questions.explanation: `gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID` writes the active project into the configuration and `gcloud config set compute/region REGION` writes the default Compute Engine region. The two commands can be chained with `;` and persist in the active named configuration. `gcloud init` is interactive and does not accept `--skip-prompts`. `gcloud configure` is not a real subcommand. `gcloud set` is missing the required `config` keyword.
